messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-six years old when he came to the intake session, and he carried himself with the careful deliberation of someone who had learned, long ago, that sudden movements draw attention. He was a detective with the city police department—a position that had once seemed like an act of redemption, a way to stand on the side of protection rather than vulnerability. His wife, Priya, had encouraged him to seek help after she found him, for the third time in a month, asleep in the armchair at two in the morning with the television still playing, his laptop open beside him to a work file he had not actually been reading.

The trauma itself dated back forty years, to a childhood in a household where his father's violence had been as unpredictable as weather. Rajesh's earliest coherent memory was of being seven years old, standing in the kitchen while his father's hand—large, calloused, and warm from the stove he had just been using—came down across his shoulder. The heat of that contact had burned into him in a way that transcended the physical injury. What remained lodged in his nervous system was not just the pain but the specific sensation: the warmth of skin against skin, the knowledge that something hot could come at him without warning, the terrible intimacy of being hurt by someone who was supposed to keep him safe. Over the decades, Rajesh had learned that certain temperatures—the precise warmth of another person's hand on his shoulder, the heat radiating from a radiator, even the specific warmth of his own body under blankets in the dark—could send him spiraling into a state of acute dread.

The other triggers had accumulated differently. Doors had always been dangerous; his father's arrival home had been announced by the sound of the front door opening, and later, by the slamming of interior doors as his father moved through the house in escalating anger. Now, at thirty-six, Rajesh found himself flinching at the sound of any door in motion, whether at home or at the precinct. He had taken to keeping his office door open during his shifts, a choice that had begun to isolate him professionally; colleagues interpreted it as a lack of focus, and supervisors had started to question whether he was suited for detailed casework that required concentration. What they could not see was that a closed door, to Rajesh, was a prelude to something unbearable.

The sleeping alone had emerged more recently, crystallizing over the past two years into something that had begun to fracture his marriage. When Priya traveled for her work as a consultant, Rajesh could not remain in their bedroom. He would wait until she left, then migrate to the couch, to the armchair, to the kitchen table—anywhere but the dark, enclosed space where he had to surrender consciousness. He had come to believe that sleep itself was a form of helplessness, and that sleeping alone was a form of abandonment to forces he could not control. The few times he had tried to push through and lie in bed without her, he had lasted perhaps an hour before panic seized him and he was forced to get up, turn on every light in the house, and wait for dawn.

Over the past year, Rajesh's world had contracted. He had stopped going to the gym where he used to swim, stopped attending the monthly dinners with his extended family, stopped accepting invitations from colleagues. Being around people required a kind of presence he could no longer muster; he was afraid of what they might see in him, or worse, what he might involuntarily do or say that would reveal the damage underneath. He had come to believe that there was something fundamentally defective about him—not just his reactions, but his essential self. His inability to sleep normally, to be touched without flinching, to sit comfortably in a room with a closed door, all of it pointed to a single conclusion: he was broken in ways that could not be fixed. The detective who was supposed to protect others could not even protect himself from his own past.

Priya had finally insisted on the appointment after finding him at three in the morning, still in his work clothes, staring at nothing. She had said, quietly, that she was losing him. Rajesh knew she was right. What frightened him most was not that he would never recover, but that recovery might require him to feel the things he had spent forty years trying to outrun.
